beats.headline: Why is your CI runner a security liability?
beats.subline: Mounting the Docker socket is a root-level backdoor.
beats.narration: Running docker build inside your CI pipeline is a security nightmare. Whether it is Docker-in-Docker or mounting the host socket, you are essentially handing root access to every build job.

beats.title: Daemon vs Daemonless

top.label: Traditional Docker
top.code:
docker build -t app:v1 .
# Requires --privileged
# Access to /var/run/docker.sock

bottom.label: Google Jib
bottom.code:
./mvnw jib:build
# Pure Java execution
# No Docker daemon

beats.narration: Traditional builds require a privileged daemon. Jib is different. It is a Java library that speaks directly to the registry API, keeping your CI environment isolated and secure.

beats.title: Jib's Daemonless Pipeline
beats.subtitle: Direct Registry Communication
beats.narration: Jib skips the daemon entirely. It compiles your code, packages OCI layers in memory, and pushes them straight to your container registry using standard HTTPS. No Docker CLI required.

beats.title: The Build Command
beats.caption: No Dockerfile needed
beats.narration: Notice we run compile, not package. Jib reads your classes and dependencies directly from the build output, so you never waste time building a fat JAR.

beats.title: Part 1 Locked In
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next (Part 2): How Jib optimizes layer caching →
beats.narration: That is the security foundation. In Part 2, we look at how Jib optimizes your image layers to make builds lightning fast.

beats.headline: Why does a 1-line code change re-upload 100MB?
beats.subline: Fat JARs are the enemy of efficient CI caching.
beats.narration: If you use a fat JAR, a one-line code change invalidates the entire archive. Jib solves this by splitting your application into four intelligent layers.

beats.title: Jib's 4-Layer Stack
beats.subtitle: Optimized for incremental updates
beats.narration: Jib separates your code from your dependencies. When you change logic, only the tiny classes layer is re-uploaded. The massive dependency layer stays cached in the registry.

beats.title: Gradle Configuration

steps.explanation: Hardened base image with no shell or package manager.
Numeric UID 65532 satisfies K8s security policies.

beats.narration: Use a Distroless base image. It lacks a shell, making it harder for attackers to move laterally. Setting the user to 65532 ensures you pass Kubernetes non-root security checks.

beats.title: Reproducible Builds
beats.caption: Deterministic SHA-256 digests
beats.narration: Jib makes builds reproducible by normalizing timestamps to the Unix epoch. If your source code hasn't changed, the resulting image digest will be identical every single time.

beats.title: Part 2 Locked In
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next (Part 3): Multi-arch support without QEMU →
beats.narration: Now you have fast, reproducible builds. In Part 3, we look at how to build multi-architecture images without needing slow QEMU emulation.

beats.headline: Why is your build slow on ARM64?
beats.subline: QEMU emulation is killing your build performance.
beats.narration: Building for both x86 and ARM64 usually means slow QEMU emulation. Jib bypasses this entirely because it does not execute native binaries during the build process.

beats.title: Multi-Platform Config

steps.explanation: Jib creates a multi-arch manifest automatically.

beats.narration: Just define your platforms in the plugin config. Jib builds the layers once and creates a manifest list. It is fast, native, and requires zero extra infrastructure.

beats.title: Emulation vs Native Jib
beats.narration: Buildx relies on emulation to build for different architectures. Jib simply assembles the OCI tarballs in memory, making it significantly faster for multi-platform support.

beats.title: CI Integration
beats.caption: Simple GitHub Action
beats.narration: In your CI, just pass the image tag as an environment variable. Jib handles the rest, pushing a clean, immutable image to your registry.

beats.title: Part 3 Locked In
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next (Part 4): Jib vs Buildpacks vs Dockerfiles →
beats.narration: You are now a Jib expert. In Part 4, we compare Jib against Buildpacks and traditional Dockerfiles to see when you should use each.

beats.headline: Jib, Buildpacks, or Dockerfiles?
beats.subline: The right tool depends on your OS requirements.
beats.narration: Jib is great, but it is not a silver bullet. When do you choose Jib over Buildpacks or a standard Dockerfile?

beats.title: Tooling Trade-offs
beats.narration: Jib is perfect for pure JVM microservices. But if your app needs native system libraries like ffmpeg, stick with a multi-stage Dockerfile.

beats.title: Decision Matrix
beats.subtitle: Pick the right tool
beats.narration: If your app is pure Java, Jib is the winner. If you need native GraalVM images, look at Buildpacks. If you need custom system packages, use a Dockerfile.

beats.title: Final Summary
beats.caption: Mastering containerization
beats.narration: Jib is the gold standard for secure, fast JVM containerization. It removes the daemon, optimizes layers, and keeps your CI pipeline clean.
